comment: Defects found in this repository's own skills and installer.

bugs.title: The shipped core library lost plan_stat_mode and plan_stat_uid, so an installed skill could not read a file mode
bugs.reproduce: bash planning/scripts/build-plan-libs.sh; grep -c "^plan_stat_mode()" planning/scripts/plan-core-lib.sh
bugs.observed: 0 definitions. Two tests said so: test-portable-helpers.sh reported plan_stat_mode: command not found for three assertions, and test-duplication-ratchet.sh reported it is referenced by MAINTAINER.md section 3 but no longer exists.
bugs.expected: Both helpers present in the compiled library; plan_atomic_write calls plan_stat_mode to preserve a file mode.
bugs.mechanism: The re-marking script kept PACKAGE: DEV on any path matching *probe* -- intended for a planted test fixture named plan_probe_dev_only.sh -- and planning/scripts/lib/core/plan_stat_probe.sh matched on its name. PACKAGE: DEV means dev-build-only, so the prod build excluded it.
bugs.fix: Marked plan_stat_probe.sh PACKAGE: PROD and rebuilt. Every other compiler input was checked for the same mistake; it was the only one.
bugs.verification: test-portable-helpers.sh and test-duplication-ratchet.sh both pass; five stat-helper definitions and calls are back in plan-core-lib.sh. Re-marking the file PACKAGE: DEV reproduces the failure.
bugs.found_by: the both-shell run of the release commit, on both bash 5.3 and 3.2
bugs.notes: A name-substring match standing in for a marker. The marker was right in every file; the script that wrote it guessed from the filename. It also shows the release checks were not sufficient on their own: build-release.sh --list and a by-hand diff of npm pack both passed a library with a function missing, because they compare file sets and not file contents.

bugs.title: test-plan-overview fails on both macOS legs and reports nothing, so the PR is red with no diagnosis
bugs.reproduce: CI run 32726302448 on PR #3 (head f699f84). Both macOS jobs: 96 ran, 95 passed, 1 failed -- test-plan-overview, exit 1. ubuntu-latest passes all 96, and ./verify-both-shells.sh passes 96/96 on bash 5.3 and bash 3.2 on Linux.
bugs.observed: The only output under the FAIL line is the limited-run wrapper's memlimit warnings. No assertion text, no t_end summary, and no sed/awk/grep error anywhere in the full job log.
bugs.expected: Either the test passes on macOS, or it says which assertion failed.
bugs.mechanism: Confirmed by the speaking trap on CI run 32751254496: test-plan-overview.sh line 90 called timeout(9) on render-plan-overview --watch, and macOS does not ship timeout (the B6 class). The watcher died instantly of exit 127, watch.log stayed empty, grep -c exited 1 under pipefail+set -e, and the ERR trap named the exact line — the diagnosis the first half of the fix was built to produce.
bugs.fix: this session — the watch case bounds itself by polling for the second render (no timeout binary); chat/tests/test-chat.sh swaps its one timeout(5) for a read -t loop with the same ceiling; render-plan-overview traps TERM/INT so a stopped watcher exits promptly instead of deferring the signal behind its sleep child
bugs.verification: PR #3 run 32756400447: both macOS legs pass 97/97 with test-plan-overview green on macOS system bash 3.2 and the runner default bash — first macOS pass since the renderer landed. Linux unchanged.
bugs.found_by: CI on PR #3, opened for exactly this reason: 46 commits with 88 files changed had never run on BSD userland, and the branch itself had just made the macOS legs blocking
bugs.notes: Blocking because -ox removed continue-on-error from both macOS legs (T37), so this fails the PR rather than being informational. Diagnose it on a runner, not by reading: stop discarding the setup commands' output first -- capture and print it on failure -- and the cause will name itself. Worth checking the same pattern in the other new tests from this branch, since a setup command redirected to /dev/null hides a BSD failure the same way anywhere it appears. Order of work: make the test able to speak before fixing what it fails on -- capture the setup commands' output and print it on failure -- then push and read the macOS leg rather than reading the code. The same discarded-output pattern is worth checking in the other tests this branch added: test-add-work-unit-staging, test-adversarial-review-mint-order, test-adversarial-review-preamble, test-function-length-ratchet, test-installer-opencode-permissions, test-owned-roster-scaffold, test-verifier-reach-memo and chat/tests/test-chat.sh. And the flag cannot go back: making those legs blocking is what caught this.

bugs.title: The chat tests wait for a 'chat serving:' banner the detached server never prints, so every detached instance times out as not-ready
bugs.reproduce: cd src/chat && cargo build && cd ../.. && h=$(mktemp -d /tmp/t.XXXXX) && ./src/chat/target/debug/chat serve --home "$h" --bind 127.0.0.1 --port 17901 >"$h/serve.log" 2>&1 & sleep 1; case "$(cat "$h/serve.log")" in *"chat serving:"*) echo MATCH;; *) echo 'NO MATCH';; esac
bugs.observed: Prints 'NO MATCH'. The log holds 94 bytes: 'chat serving (detached): tcp 127.0.0.1:17901 pid 1146894 [endpoint given on the command line]'. The server is healthy — it binds, serves and answers clients — but the needle 'chat serving:' cannot occur in it. Both chat suites hang on this: test-chat-binary.sh:94 and test-chat-config.sh:386,417 all wait for that exact substring. test-chat-binary reports 'the server never reported serving on 17811. Its output:' followed by nothing, and test-chat-config reports FAIL (8) — every one of the eight downstream of a server that never became ready.
bugs.expected: The readiness probe recognises a server that is in fact serving, in each of the three banner forms the binary emits.
bugs.mechanism: src/chat/src/main.rs prints three different banners: line 2729 'chat serving: {} ({}), run dir {} [{}]' for the attached case, and lines 2622 and 2632 'chat serving (detached, unregistered): ...' and 'chat serving (detached): ...' for the two detached ones. The tests match the literal 'chat serving:' — with the colon immediately after 'serving' — so only the attached form is recognised, and every detached start reads as never-ready. The tests are the side that is wrong about the contract, but note test-chat-binary.sh:77-84 carries a comment explaining that the readiness probe must never be the thing under test; matching a banner's exact punctuation is the same coupling in a different place.
bugs.fix: Not fixed — every surface was deleted. chat/tests/test-chat-binary.sh, chat/tests/test-chat-config.sh and src/chat/src/main.rs went with 6bba241, "chat: ship two binaries per skill; drop src/chat; rewire CI for the rust workspace". The detached-server readiness handshake the bug is about no longer exists: chat/tests/ holds only test-chat.sh and test-chat-resolution.sh, and neither waits for a banner — readiness is the server writing server.port, which the tests poll for.
bugs.verification: The string "chat serving" now occurs exactly once in the whole of master, inside this BUGS.json entry describing the bug. No live file names it. All three recorded surfaces are absent from master's tree.
bugs.found_by: main session, diagnosing the two red tests that block Phase 1 of the 2.0.0-alpha release
bugs.notes: Filed as urgent/blocking, which distorted the register's priority ordering for as long as it sat open against deleted code. Closing it is the point of the sweep that found it: a stale entry at the top of the queue is worse than no entry, because everything below it is judged relative to it. Found by checking every open entry's surfaces against master rather than by anyone reading the entry.

bugs.title: The release-package gate rejects any prerelease version, so bumping package.json to 2.0.0-alpha turns the suite red
bugs.reproduce: for v in 2.0.0 2.0.0-alpha 2.0.0-alpha.1; do printf '%-16s %s\n' "$v" "$(printf '%s' "$v" | grep -c '^[0-9][0-9.]*[0-9]$')"; done
bugs.observed: 2.0.0 -> 1, 2.0.0-alpha -> 0, 2.0.0-alpha.1 -> 0. tests/test-release-package.sh:37-39 reads the version out of package.json and asserts that count is '1', so any version carrying a prerelease identifier fails 'package.json states a version' and the whole gate goes red.
bugs.expected: The gate accepts the versions the project actually intends to publish, prerelease identifiers included, while still rejecting a missing or malformed one.
bugs.mechanism: The pattern '^[0-9][0-9.]*[0-9]$' was written when every released version was numeric — the tag list is v1.0.0 through v1.4.2, none with a suffix — so nothing had ever exercised a prerelease. It anchors both ends and permits only digits and dots, which excludes the hyphen semver requires for a prerelease. This is a latent gate, not a regression: it has been correct for every version shipped so far and becomes wrong the first time an alpha is cut.
bugs.fix: 9e8ddc1 + 9ee5278 — release-package now validates full SemVer core, prerelease and build metadata forms, including numeric prerelease leading-zero rules and combined prerelease/build cases
bugs.verification: The gate accepts 2.0.0-alpha, 2.0.0-alpha.1, 2.0.0-alpha.1+build.7 and 2.0.0+build.7, while rejecting 2.0, x.y.z, empty, 02.0.0, 2.0.0-, 2.0.0-01 and 2.0.0-alpha..1. The release-package integration test passes from the real-disk worktree; a no-op guard mutation fails its assertions.
bugs.found_by: main session, working out the runbook for tagging 2.0.0-alpha; found before the bump rather than after, so it has never actually gone red

bugs.title: interactive-shell-input named cursor keys are case-sensitive and ignore application cursor mode
bugs.reproduce: Run mc in the wrapper, then submit key up or key UP while mc has enabled application cursor mode.
bugs.observed: Lowercase names were rejected. Uppercase cursor names were acknowledged but sent the normal cursor sequence, which mc rendered as literal input instead of moving the selected row.
bugs.expected: Named keys are discoverable without case assumptions and cursor sequences match the terminal mode requested by the active application.
bugs.mechanism: key_sequence only recognized uppercase names, and the screen parser did not retain the private cursor-mode flag set by applications with DECSET.
bugs.fix: Working tree change — normalize named keys and encode cursor keys as SS3 when application cursor mode is active
bugs.verification: Unit tests cover lowercase named keys and DECSET/DECRST application cursor mode; cargo test --locked passes.
bugs.found_by: fresh agent protocol run, subworker Gauss
bugs.notes: This was the direct blocker for navigating mc's visible file pane.

bugs.title: interactive-shell emits stale or corrupted parent-shell screen state after subprocess exit
bugs.reproduce: Start one wrapper-owned interactive Bash, launch and exit nano or mc, then observe the parent shell after the child lifecycle transition.
bugs.observed: The agent saw stale command fragments interleaved with the restored Bash prompt after nano and mc exited; the wrapper later reported child_exit but emitted a very large burst of buffered screen JSON before that lifecycle event.
bugs.expected: After a subprocess exits, the next observation is a coherent current parent-shell screen, and lifecycle ordering is explicit enough that an agent can distinguish the restored shell from stale child output.
bugs.mechanism: The PTY reader publishes each read as a screen delta while the terminal model processes redraws and alternate-screen restoration incrementally; child exit and buffered PTY bytes are not synchronized into a post-transition snapshot boundary.
bugs.found_by: fresh agent protocol run, subworker Socrates
bugs.notes: The autowrap fix addresses one renderer corruption mechanism but does not yet prove subprocess-transition synchronization is correct.

bugs.title: The registers guard and its test use the banned python3-shipped construct, so the portability gate fails on master
bugs.reproduce: ./planning/tests/test-portability-contract.sh
bugs.observed: portability: ./.github/registers-guard.sh uses banned construct 'python3-shipped' at line 101, and the same for ./.github/tests/test-registers-guard.sh at line 91. test-portability-contract FAILs, and master's ubuntu-latest leg is red with it (run 33873690073).
bugs.expected: The gate passes. python3 in a CI-only tree is either allowlisted for this rule or replaced, but master is not left red.
bugs.mechanism: The guard calls python3 for the duplicate-id check that a textual merge cannot detect, and its own comment argues CODE-STYLE.md permits python3 for development tooling. Assertion 4 of test-portability-contract scans every TRACKED script for a detectable banned construct, and .github/ carries no allowlist row, so that justification was never expressed anywhere the gate can read it. The rule's own replacement text anticipates the case: probe sites, the generated installer tables and dev-only trees carry allowlist rows.
bugs.fix: e34a7485 on fix/master-red-trio (PR #56) -- ./.github/*:python3-shipped joins the dev-only allowlist group the rule's own replacement text provides for
bugs.verification: test-portability-contract PASS. Mutation: a python3 line appended to planning/scripts/plan-env.sh, a SHIPPED file, is still reported, so the row exempts one dev-only tree rather than disabling the rule.
bugs.found_by: master CI run 33873690073, ubuntu-latest leg; reproduced locally

bugs.title: Declaring chat's runtimes puts python3 into the generated install.sh, which the python3-shipped gate bans
bugs.reproduce: bash planning/tests/test-portability-contract.sh   # at fa1bd62
bugs.observed: portability: ./install.sh uses banned construct 'python3-shipped' at line 417 -- see PORTABILITY.md. install.sh:417 is the generated members table: @server-runtimes) case "$platform" in *:*) printf '%s\n' python3 node perl socat ;; esac ;;
bugs.expected: Either declaring an optional runtime is allowed, or the gate says why it is not, but the suite is not red for doing the thing T39 asked for.
bugs.mechanism: e6492f6 declared the any-of group in chat/requires.tsv, and installer/build.sh generates the requirement tables into install.sh, so the literal python3 now appears in the shipped installer. The portability gate scans every tracked *.sh including the generated install.sh, and its allowlist exempts only ./chat/scripts/chat-server.sh and ./chat/tests/test-chat.sh. So the declaration the brief asked for is exactly what trips the rule.
bugs.fix: 4befd4e — exact-file allowlist row ./install.sh:python3-shipped in test-portability-contract: the generated tables NAME optional runtimes to verify and hint them, which is not requiring one; strength still decides
bugs.verification: test-portability-contract passes on both legs; removing the row restores both findings. The rule-vs-gate question itself stays open as T40.
bugs.found_by: the 5-minute watch: CI run 32728982657 showed ubuntu failing two tests rather than the one already recorded, and it reproduces locally
bugs.notes: This is T40 arriving as a blocker rather than a discussion. Do not reach for an allowlist row on install.sh: that file is generated from every skill's requires.tsv, so exempting it turns the rule off for anything any skill ever declares. The rule text is what is wrong -- it is named python3-shipped and it means do not depend on python3, while what it detects is the word appearing in a shell file. Naming an optional runtime in a fallback chain is not depending on it. Options, cheapest first: narrow the detect so it matches an invocation rather than the bare word; or scope the rule to hard requirements and let a soft or grouped declaration through; or rescope it to shipped runtime code, which is the case it was written for and which no *.sh scan can see anyway (chat/runtime/server.py has always been invisible to it).

bugs.title: A goal with no bare work-unit ids in its roster aborts validate-plan, which exits 1 with no verdict
bugs.reproduce: cp -R .plans/harden-test-reporting-and-plan-dir /tmp/rost/plan; g=/tmp/rost/plan/01-plan-dir-synonym/goal.md; grep -v '^`W[0-9]' "$g" > "$g.n" && mv "$g.n" "$g"; bash planning/scripts/validate-plan.sh /tmp/rost/plan; echo "exit $?"
bugs.observed: exit 1 with four FAIL lines and no summary at all -- no "Plan validation failed with N error(s)." and no "passed" line. bash -x ends: printf '%s\n%s\n' '' '' / grep -E '^W[0-9][0-9]+$' / sort -u / tr, then roster_ids= followed immediately by plan_validate_cleanup, which is the EXIT trap rather than the next pass.
bugs.expected: A goal whose roster names no unit is a finding or a warning, and the run still reports its verdict.
bugs.mechanism: validate-plan-propagation-lib.sh:347 assigns from a pipeline: roster_ids="$(printf ... | grep -E '^W[0-9][0-9]+$' | sort -u | tr '\n' ' ')". With both awk passes empty the printf emits two blank lines, grep matches nothing and exits 1, pipefail makes that the pipeline's status, the assignment inherits it, and set -e aborts the script -- before the summary and before every later pass. The reporter saw the WARN-only variant, which is the same abort in a plan whose earlier passes had produced no FAIL lines; the missing summary is the signature either way.
bugs.fix: this session — the roster_ids pipeline guards its grep with || true inside a brace group, the same escape every sibling assignment in the file already uses; an empty match is an answer, not an error
bugs.verification: New empty-roster case in test-roster-cross-reference.sh: stripping the bare WNN blurbs must still produce roster-omits findings and a Plan validation failed verdict. Mutation: reverting to the unguarded grep fails with "the roster check never ran" — exactly the missing-summary signature.
bugs.found_by: an active worker on the installed skill, hitting it on goal 05; reproduced here against the current tree
bugs.notes: Worse than a wrong verdict: the run reports none, and every pass after the roster is skipped silently, so a plan can be far more broken than the output suggests. A guard on that assignment is the immediate fix, but the class deserves the gate -- PORTABILITY.md already bans `| grep -q` under pipefail for the SIGPIPE variant, and this is its sibling: a grep whose empty result is the ordinary case, inside an assignment, under set -e. A first fix-probe here added || true and appeared not to help, which was a botched edit rather than evidence; the bash -x trace is what settled the mechanism.

bugs.title: subagent worktrees are reused for new tasks, so a fresh worker inherits the previous task's stale base commit
bugs.reproduce: Launch any subagent with isolation: worktree, then in its worktree run: git log --oneline -1; git rev-list --count HEAD..origin/refactor/portability-and-installer-ox
bugs.observed: Two subagents launched within one hour on 2026-08-28 both started behind the branch tip: the webview worker by 354 commits, based on de02b9f — a tree where planning/scripts/overview-*.sh and planning/templates/ do not exist at all — and the chatfix worker by 352. Both reported it themselves and reset to the tip before reading anything. T35 records the same defect and is marked done.
bugs.expected: A worktree created for a subagent starts at the commit the launching session is on, so the worker sees the files it was sent to change.
bugs.mechanism: Established by Tschallacka, who knows the harness: old worktrees are REUSED for new tasks rather than created fresh. A worktree left behind by a finished subagent is handed to the next one, so the new agent inherits whatever commit the previous task stopped at — which is why the three today started 354, 352 and 358 commits behind rather than at the tip, and why the distances differed. My entry recorded 'Not established here' and guessed at creation; the defect is in what happens at the END of a task, not the beginning. A worktree that is cleaned up after its merge cannot be inherited stale by anyone.
bugs.fix: git-worktrees/SKILL.md § Merging the work back: removal is stated as the task's last step, covering the no-merge case (abandoned work, a checkout only ever used to look at something) as well as the merged one, with the reuse consequence spelled out as the reason; docs/README.md carries the short form. Applied to this session's six worktrees, all confirmed clean and 0 commits ahead of HEAD before removal, and their five orphaned worktree-agent-* branches deleted.
bugs.verification: Partial, and stated as such. Verified: 'git worktree list' now returns one line, the main checkout, so there is no worktree left for a next task to inherit; all six removals were preceded by a dirty/untracked count of 0 and 'git rev-list --count HEAD..<branch>' of 0, so nothing was discarded. NOT yet verified: that a subagent launched with isolation: worktree now starts at the tip. That observation needs a real launch and is the mutation that would fail without the fix — the next subagent this repo launches supplies it, and B77 stays confirmed until it does.
bugs.found_by: main session, from two independent subagent reports in one hour; both workers only noticed because their briefs told them to check
bugs.notes: Third occurrence the same day: the plancrypt worker started 358 commits behind and reset to 9be8d1a. That is three of three subagent worktrees launched in this session — webview 354 behind, chatfix 352, plancrypt 358 — so the failure rate is not intermittent, it is universal. All three caught it only because their briefs carried an explicit instruction to check the base commit, which means the current mitigation is a sentence I have to remember to write into every brief. A worker launched without it reads a tree that predates the feature it was sent to change. The fix follows from the mechanism: when a subagent finishes and its worktree has no other purpose, remove it once its branch is merged — if a merge applies at all. That closes the reuse path at the point where the worktree becomes garbage, rather than trying to detect staleness at the point where it is handed out. Cleaning up is also the cheaper half: a stale-base check has to run in every brief and be remembered by every author, while a removal happens once, by whoever did the merge and is already looking at the branch. The title carried the disproven cause ('still created from a stale commit') and was corrected in place, since bug-update.sh has no --title; register-rebuild.sh bugs reports the file stamped, sorted and sound afterwards.

bugs.title: interactive-shell-input text rejects spaces instead of sending one text payload
bugs.reproduce: src/interactive-shell/target/debug/interactive-shell-input --socket <socket> text 'Hello World'
bugs.observed: The helper rejects the second word with 'unknown argument: World'. Sending separate text requests produces 'HelloWorld', so the agent cannot enter ordinary spaced text through the documented text operation.
bugs.expected: A text operation accepts one complete payload, including spaces, and writes that payload to the interactive process.
bugs.mechanism: The CLI parser treats every token after the operation as a new top-level argument; it does not preserve the caller's intended text payload as the remainder of the command.
bugs.fix: 77c29cb — text and paste consume the remaining CLI payload and preserve spaces
bugs.verification: Protocol test cli_text_preserves_spaces_and_input_help_is_available invokes interactive-shell-input text Hello World against a live PTY and observes the spaced payload; cargo test passes.
bugs.found_by: fresh agent protocol run, subworker Halley/Godel evaluation
bugs.notes: This blocked creation of the required test content and forced a workaround. Quoting alone does not help because the helper receives already-split process arguments.

bugs.title: interactive-shell screen observations do not expose mc pane focus or selection changes reliably
bugs.reproduce: Start interactive Bash through the wrapper, run mc without a startup directory, navigate a file pane toward /tmp with keyboard navigation, and observe after each acknowledged request.
bugs.observed: Several navigation requests returned an acknowledgement but no screen delta that identified the changed selection or focused pane. The agent reached the root listing but could not reliably activate /tmp from the observed state.
bugs.expected: An observation after an accepted navigation action makes the active pane, current directory, selected row, and focus change inferable, even when the application redraws only a cursor or attribute.
bugs.mechanism: The terminal model publishes changed row text, but does not expose cursor/focus semantics for TUI selections when the visible text remains unchanged or when the redraw is encoded primarily through terminal attributes.
bugs.fix: Working tree change — expose reverse-video selection as highlighted=true on observed text hints
bugs.verification: Screen elements now distinguish verified actionability from reverse-video highlight state; unit coverage verifies a highlighted text run. Active-pane semantics remain intentionally heuristic.
bugs.found_by: fresh agent protocol run, subworker Godel
bugs.notes: This is specifically an unknown-TUI navigation defect; the new highlight hint improves selection discovery, but the generic model still cannot prove application focus.

bugs.title: interactive-shell observations do not identify color-based TUI selection
bugs.reproduce: Start mc through an interactive Bash wrapper, navigate its file pane, and request view or observe after a selection change.
bugs.observed: mc changes foreground/background attributes for the selected row rather than reverse video. The agent receives changed text or styles but no reliable selected-row or focus hint.
bugs.expected: The observation makes a probable visual selection distinguishable, with an explicit heuristic/confidence marker that does not claim application-level certainty.
bugs.mechanism: The wrapper exposes raw style spans and only maps reverse video to highlighted=true; it does not compare row-level color changes or identify pane boundaries.
bugs.fix: Working tree change — derive highlighted=true from reverse video or a conservative adjacent-row color outlier
bugs.verification: Unit coverage verifies a color-outlier selection hint, and a live mc observation identifies the selected file-pane row; the field remains explicitly heuristic.
bugs.found_by: fresh unknown-TUI validation, subworker Wegener
bugs.notes: This is an app-agnostic inference problem. Any fix must remain a heuristic and expose confidence rather than asserting mc semantics.

bugs.title: register-read.sh ships to users but the library it sources does not, so it dies on first use
bugs.reproduce: Build the prod file list and copy just those files, then run the reader: bash -c 'source installer/src/50-manifest.sh; SOURCE_ROOT=. skill_files planning prod' | grep register-   # lists scripts/register-read.sh and NOT scripts/register-lib.sh. Copy the prod list into an empty tree and run: BUGS_JSON=/tmp/b.json scripts/register-read.sh bug count
bugs.observed: register-read.sh: line 32: <dir>/register-lib.sh: No such file or directory. The reader is MODE: PROD and sits in the planning prod arm; register-lib.sh is MODE: DEV and sits in the dev arm, so a prod install receives the reader without it.
bugs.expected: A shipped script's dependencies ship with it. Either register-lib.sh becomes MODE: PROD and joins the prod arm, or register-read.sh stops being shipped.
bugs.mechanism: The two markers disagree and nothing cross-checks a shipped script against what it sources. tests/test-mode-markers.sh compares each file's marker against skill_files() membership, which both files satisfy individually - the reader is PROD and listed prod, the library is DEV and listed dev - so the pair is consistent by that test's rule while being unusable together. CODE-STYLE.md's own instruction is that a missing library is a broken install and must fail loudly, which is exactly what happens; nobody had run the shipped copy.
bugs.found_by: T81 work, maintainer session 2026-09-01
bugs.notes: Re-confirmed on master at f4e7239 on 2026-09-02, still unfixed, and it is live on this machine rather than theoretical: /home/mdibbets/ai/agents/skills/planning/scripts/register-read.sh --help dies with "line 32: .../scripts/register-lib.sh: No such file or directory", and register-lib.sh is absent from the installed tree. Found again independently during an adversarial review round, which means it will bite the next helper call any agent makes. Confirmed with the repository's own manifest function, which is the authoritative split: `bash -c 'source installer/src/50-manifest.sh; SOURCE_ROOT=. skill_files planning prod'` lists scripts/register-command.sh and scripts/register-read.sh and NOT scripts/register-lib.sh, while the dev arm lists register-lib.sh and register-rebuild.sh. Master's register-read.sh still sources the library unconditionally at line 32, so a prod install cannot work. NEW SURFACE not in the list above: planning/PACKAGE-MANIFEST.tsv holds exactly two register rows - register-command.sh and register-read.sh - and omits register-lib.sh AND register-rebuild.sh entirely. So the pair is inconsistent in three places, not two, and CODE-STYLE.md section 3's rule that the four places move together is broken. That also means tests/test-skill-files-manifest.sh and tests/test-installer-manifest.sh should be failing on this pair and are not, which is a second defect worth checking while fixing this one. Installing the newest planning helper from the repository does NOT resolve it, since master reproduces the arms exactly as described.

bugs.title: No helper can set a UI story's Status or Evidence, so a story can be run but never recorded and the completion gate can never pass
bugs.reproduce: t=$(mktemp -d)/plan; cp -r .plans/<a plan with ui-user-stories.md> "$t"; chmod 600 "$t/.env"; s=planning/scripts; "$s/update-ui-story.sh" "$t" US-01 --expected probe; awk -F'|' '/^\| US-01 /{print "status cell:" $7}' "$t/ui-user-stories.md"; "$s/update-plan-content.sh" -tp "$t" stories 1.1 9 '"a","b","c","d","e","f","g","h","i"'; "$s/update-plan-content.sh" -f "$t" stories Status passed
bugs.observed: update-ui-story.sh prints 'Updated US-01' and the status cell still reads '💤 untested' -- it writes only persona, actions, interaction and expected. update-plan-content.sh -tp refuses with 'Paragraph was not found exactly once: § 1.1', because ui-user-stories.md is a bare heading plus a table with no numbered paragraph to address. -f refuses with 'Field was not found exactly once: Status', because Status is a table column and not a field line. No other helper writes the file.
bugs.expected: A sanctioned writer for the two columns that record a run: Status, from the documented vocabulary (untested, in progress, passed, bug found, user-approved excluded), and Evidence. The natural home is update-ui-story.sh, which already addresses a story by id and rewrites its row.
bugs.mechanism: ui-user-stories.md is written by add-ui-story.sh and amended by update-ui-story.sh, whose flags are --persona, --actions, --interaction and --expected only. The generic content writers cannot reach it: -tp addresses a numbered paragraph and the file has none, and -f addresses a '- Label: value' field line while Status is a table cell. The run cache at ui-story-runs/US-NN.md is worse off -- it has a 'Run result' section with its own '- Status:' line, and no document id at all in plan-document-lib.sh, so no content writer can address it either. Meanwhile the UI reference makes every applicable story passing a condition of completion and validate-plan --complete enforces it, so the gate depends on a value nothing can set. bugs.title: The bug-report skill's documented validation snippet uses IN/1, which rjq cannot parse, so it prints "BUGS.json is sound" for any file
bugs.reproduce:
echo '{}' | rjq 'if ("a" | IN("a","b")) then "yes" else "no" end'
# then run the Validating the file snippet from bug-report/SKILL.md with rjq in place of jq, against any BUGS.json
bugs.observed: rjq exits 5 with [(File { code: ... }, [("IN", Filter(1))])] and writes nothing to stdout. Every caller treats that empty stdout as the sound case. Measured against a register carrying a duplicate id and two invalid statuses: pre-push-check.sh printed "ok BUGS.json parses, ids unique, statuses known" and found nothing. jq on the same expression returns the three findings. The shipped reg_findings helper, on the same file, reports all of them.
bugs.expected: Either the snippet runs under rjq, or a runtime that cannot evaluate it fails loudly instead of reporting the register sound.
bugs.mechanism: rjq is jaq-based and jaq does not define jq's IN/1 builtin. The snippet uses it four times (parent existence, status, severity, priority). Command substitution discards the parse error to stderr and yields an empty string, and the snippet's success test is emptiness of that string -- so a runtime failure and a clean register are indistinguishable. The skill's own note that `jq -e` is wrong here because it exits 4 on empty output shows the empty-means-sound convention was deliberate; it just has no guard for the command not having run.
bugs.fix: pre-push-check.sh section 5 deletes its own copy and delegates to reg_findings, and a check that cannot run is now a failure rather than silence. bug-report/SKILL.md and todo/SKILL.md express the same rules with index(...) instead of IN/1, bind each entry with `as $e` first, and test the command status before trusting empty output.
bugs.verification: Both snippets extracted verbatim from their SKILL.md and run under rjq against copies: the real BUGS.json and TODO.json report sound (exit 0), and a register carrying a duplicate id, a dangling parent and invalid status/severity/priority yields all five findings. Before the fix the same expressions exited 5 with empty stdout, which every caller read as sound. The pre-push half was mutation-tested separately: a duplicate id in BUGS.json now yields "BUGS.json: duplicate ids" where the old check printed "ok ... ids unique, statuses known". The mutation that fails without the fix is restoring IN/1: rjq exits 5, and the added status guard turns that into an explicit failure instead of a false pass -- which is how the first attempt at this fix was caught, since `A | index(B)` evaluates B against A and a bare index(.status) dies with "cannot index".
bugs.found_by: running the skill's own validation after adding B115 and B116; it reported sound while rjq was erroring
bugs.notes: Found in bug-report/SKILL.md while validating B115 and B116, then found live in pre-push-check.sh, which carried its own jq-flavoured copy behind 2>/dev/null and || true. That gate had never fired on any machine using rjq -- which is every machine following the register contract, since reg_require_jq refuses with 69 without it. Held at blocking for that reason: a gate that always passes is worse than no gate, and this one runs before every push. All three surfaces are now fixed. The durable lesson is the shape rather than the builtin: empty output means sound ONLY if the command ran, so any check of this form has to test the status too. Went unnoticed because a passing gate looks identical either way. Since the fix, feature/ship-register-helpers replaced both documented snippets with `bugs check` and `todo check`, so bug-report/SKILL.md and todo/SKILL.md no longer carry an rjq expression to get wrong. The index(...) form and the status guard survive where they still run: reg_findings in planning/scripts/register-lib.sh, which pre-push-check.sh section 5 delegates to, and the two SKILL.md files now point at that oracle and restate why IN/1 cannot be used in it.

bugs.title: register-resolve.sh reads index stage 1 as the merge base, so during a rebase it reports no collisions and advises taking one side whole
bugs.reproduce: On a branch whose BUGS.json commits precede a commit that renumbers them, run: git rebase origin/master; resolve each earlier BUGS.json conflict with 'git checkout --ours -- BUGS.json && git add BUGS.json && git rebase --continue'; then at the renumbering commit run ./planning/scripts/register-resolve.sh BUGS.json

Taking theirs as advised would have dropped master's two entries entirely.
bugs.expected: Either both collisions are reported so each gets a decision, or the tool refuses to advise because index stage 1 is not the merge base of the two sides it is comparing.
bugs.mechanism: The merge base is taken from index stage 1. That is the merge base only for 'git merge'. During a rebase, stage 1 is the parent of the commit being replayed -- a commit on the branch's own history -- so an entry the OTHER side added independently appears in the base already and reads as a modification rather than an addition. The both-sides-added test therefore never fires, and the two-sided-addition case it exists to catch is reported as textual.
bugs.found_by: pr13-rescue, rebasing PR #31 onto master 16c8c06
bugs.notes: Peer of B151: both are register-resolve.sh assuming a merge where a rebase is the other half of the same workflow. B151 is the refusal's guidance naming no available action; this one is the silent wrong answer, and it is the dangerous half -- the tool exists to stop a register merge losing bug states, and here it advises exactly that. Workaround used on pr13-rescue: install the real merge base as stage 1 before running it, with 'git show $(git merge-base origin/master <branch-tip>):BUGS.json | git hash-object -w --stdin' and 'git update-index --index-info'. With that stage 1 in place it found both collisions immediately. Went unnoticed because every test and every use so far has been a merge, where stage 1 is the merge base by definition.

bugs.title: On stock macOS the registry fallback runs a real benchmark agent with no time bound at all
bugs.reproduce: On a host with neither setsid nor timeout/gtimeout: start-worker.sh calls launch_agent isolated "${WORKER_TIMEOUT:-45m}" - mode becomes registry, no timeout binary is found, and lib-agent.sh warns and launches anyway.

The watchdog polls kill -0 in one-second steps, then TERMs the ps-walked tree and escalates to KILL after 5s; wait_agent calls _agent_watchdog_stop, which kills the watchdog and its in-flight sleep. The setsid path still returns 69, and a present timeout/gtimeout still wins, so the watchdog is never used when a real bound exists.

bugs.title: dep_reaches memoizes every visited pair before exploring and reads the memo back as failure, so an earlier probe of a pair turns a later valid check into a false FAIL
bugs.reproduce: In one goal give two verification steps prose naming each other's unit id (W17 with W15 in its Depends-on cell, W15's step mentioning W17), then run validate-plan.sh <plan>. Making the bind configurable is the other, and it should not be done without deciding what protects it -- at minimum a documented warning, and the four tiers each need the change since the address is hard-coded in each. bugs.title: The overview counts only archived review rounds, so a plan whose review happened reports zero

bugs.observed: A delivered plan -- review approved, all 16 steps complete, findings 1 (0 open), 1/1 resolved -- reports review rounds 0, review depth 0/3, and a CYCLES panel reading "no review cycles recorded yet - the chart lights up after cycle 1". The same plan's adversarial-review.md carries an approved verdict and one finding row.
bugs.expected: Two rounds are always present -- the pre-implementation review and the final review -- so a plan that has been reviewed reports 2, and 3 only when a third round was actually needed. The depth ring counts against that: 2 of 2 is a complete review, not a failure against a target of 3.
bugs.mechanism: render-plan-overview.sh:153-154 sets cycles=0 and then counts '^## Cycle [0-9]' headings in adversarial-review-history.md. That file only exists once a round has been archived, which update-adversarial-review.sh does when a *new* round starts. A plan with exactly one round therefore has no history file and counts zero, and every figure derived from cycles -- the rounds count, the review-depth ring against its target of 3, and the chart -- reports as though no review occurred. The undercount is by one everywhere, and it is worst on a finished plan, where the reader concludes the work was never reviewed.
bugs.fix: this session — render-plan-overview builds one normalised cycle stream from history plus (only when no history exists) the live table, filtering placeholder rows and dropping cycles they empty; count, ring, panel and chart all read that stream, so they cannot disagree
bugs.verification: test-plan-overview pins the live-only round: one round counted, chart bar drawn, placeholder absent. Mutations: forcing cycles=0 fails the narration assertion; counting placeholder rows fails the fresh-plan placeholder assertion.
bugs.found_by: Michael, reading the delivered render: review approved and all steps complete, yet feedback and cycles empty
bugs.notes: The live round is the missing term: rounds are archived history plus the current review when one exists. Both screenshots show it -- the planning plan reports 7 findings with 0 rounds while its phase line says round 1 is open, and the delivered plan reports a resolved finding with 0 rounds. Whatever counts a round must agree with the phase line, which already says "round $((cycles + 1))" and so has the correct number in hand. Worth deciding at the same time whether review depth against a target of 3 is meaningful for a plan that needed one round and got approval; a ring reading 0/3 on an approved plan reads as a failure rather than a completed review. Corrected by Michael: the model is not "archived cycles plus the live one" but a fixed pair -- pre review and final review -- extended when the work demands another. So the count does not come from counting history headings at all; the history file says how many rounds happened beyond the pair. That also fixes the depth ring, which currently reads 0/3 on an approved plan and implies a failure: it should read 2/2 for the normal case and 3/3 when a third was needed, never a target the plan was never meant to hit.

bugs.title: install.sh with no --target exits 1 printing nothing at all, so a headless install fails silently

bash install.sh --skill git-worktrees --yes; echo "exit $?"   # exit 1, zero bytes
bash install.sh --skill git-worktrees --target "$HOME/.claude/skills" --yes; echo "exit $?"   # exit 0, installs

bugs.title: chat-send.sh's socket path lets a message body forge any nick, because newlines are not sanitised before the protocol printf
bugs.reproduce:
bash chat/scripts/chat-register.sh '#injtest'; body=$(printf 'first line from aiskills
NICK ox
PRIVMSG #injtest :this line claims to be from ox
'); bash chat/scripts/chat-send.sh '#injtest' "$body" -n aiskills --host 127.0.0.1 --port 7717; bash chat/scripts/chat-read.sh '#injtest' 0
bugs.observed: Two messages are stored from one send. Reproduced here verbatim: 'MSG #injtest 2 ... aiskills :first line from aiskills' followed by 'MSG #injtest 3 ... ox :this line claims to be from ox'. The send passed -n aiskills; message 3 is attributed to ox. A message body can forge any nick on the channel. A plain two-line body is silently truncated instead — the second line becomes a protocol command rather than text, exit stays 0, and the acknowledgement looks like success.
bugs.expected: A message body is data. Whatever it contains reaches the channel as one message attributed to the sending nick, or the send is refused.
bugs.mechanism:
chat-send.sh has two paths that disagree about sanitisation. The direct-append path runs the text through tr '
' '  ' before writing the log line. The socket path does printf 'NICK %s
PRIVMSG %s :%s
QUIT
' with the raw body, so every newline in it is a command boundary on the wire and every following line is parsed as a protocol verb. The safe path is the one callers were told not to use: B65 made --host mandatory for a message to reach subscribers at all, which routes every well-behaved caller through the unsanitised path.
bugs.fix:
fccb430 — chat-send.sh now collapses newline and carriage return to a space once, just after validation, so the socket path and the direct-append path share one sanitisation. The socket path no longer interpolates a raw body into 'NICK %s
PRIVMSG %s :%s
QUIT
'. Sanitise was chosen over refuse: refusing a body containing a newline would break the common legitimate case (an agent relaying a diff, a file excerpt, command output or a quotation — B75's own surface), and collapsing is exactly what the direct append has always done, so the two paths now agree on already-documented behaviour. Server side, a PRIVMSG rejection buys nothing against this defect because the newline IS the frame delimiter — by the time a handler sees the PRIVMSG the forged NICK is already a separate, indistinguishable, well-formed command; the python and node rungs were instead hardened to strip CR as well as LF so a bare CR cannot corrupt a stored line (the bash rung already did, perl collapses all whitespace). chat/SKILL.md now states that one message is one line.

NICK impostor
PRIVMSG #inj :forged line' as nick 'sender' on both paths and asserts one stored message, attributed to the sender, whole body on one line. Mutation: restore the pre-fix split sanitisation (drop the shared 'text=$(printf %s "$text" | tr 
 "  ")' and put the tr back inside the direct-append printf only). Observed under that mutation: FAIL 'socket path (python3): one send stored 2 messages, expected 1' and 'a body forged the nick impostor', with the log showing 'MSG #inj 2 ... sender :honest line' and 'MSG #inj 3 ... impostor :forged line'. bugs.title: chat-watch.sh never advances its cursor, so every poll re-emits the same messages

bugs.observed: Each message id is emitted once per poll for as long as the watcher runs: ids 65 and 66 each appeared 4 times in 20 seconds. Armed as a Monitor it re-delivered the same message repeatedly until the watch was stopped by hand — the first arming flooded the session with roughly a dozen copies of one message before it was noticed.
bugs.expected: Each poll prints only messages newer than the last one printed, which is what the helper's own contract says: 'using FETCH since-id so no message is missed and no message is double-read; each poll prints new messages only'.
bugs.mechanism: The since-id used for each fetch is the value the watcher started with rather than the highest id it has emitted, so every round re-requests the same window. The step-down cadence makes it worse rather than better: on a quiet channel the interval grows to 60s and the same backlog is re-emitted at each step, and any new message resets the cadence to 5s, so an active channel re-emits its whole window every five seconds.
bugs.fix: fccb430 — chat-watch.sh no longer puts --since into read_args. chat-read's argument parser is last-wins, so appending the ORIGINAL --since after the per-poll --since made every poll re-request the window the watcher started with; the starting id now lives in the cursor and nowhere else. A second mechanism was hiding behind the first: the cursor was advanced to id + 1 on the stated belief that FETCH is '>= since'. It is not — every tier's FETCH is '> since', matching the local awk '($3 + 0) > s' — so id + 1 would have silently skipped the very next message once the first bug was fixed. The cursor is now the highest id printed, taken as a max rather than from the last line so an out-of-order log cannot rewind it. The stale '>=' comment was corrected.

bugs.title: the fix-key session id falls back to a guessable value built from the pid, the whole second and bash's $RANDOM
bugs.reproduce: PATH=/usr/bin:/bin bash -c 'unset -f openssl; id="$(printf "%s-%s-%s" "$$" "$(date +%s)" "$RANDOM$RANDOM")"; printf "%s\n" "$id"'   # the arm mint-fix-keys.sh's new_session_id took whenever openssl was absent
bugs.observed: The id is three guessable fields joined by hyphens: the process id, the current time truncated to a whole second, and two draws of bash's $RANDOM. On Linux the pid space is 4194304 by default and is usually far smaller in practice; the second is known to anyone who knows roughly when the review ran; $RANDOM is a 15-bit value from a PRNG seeded per shell, giving 30 bits across the two draws. A reader who can see the fixes.md timestamps can enumerate the space.
bugs.expected: The session id comes from the OS CSPRNG or the helper refuses. It names the secret directory that gates approval, so it must not be derivable from information a claimant already has.
bugs.mechanism: new_session_id ran 'openssl rand -hex 8' and, on any failure, fell through to 'printf %s-%s-%s "$$" "$(date +%s)" "$RANDOM$RANDOM"'. The guard after it only checked the result was non-empty, which the fallback always is, so the weak arm was indistinguishable from success. openssl was declared a soft requirement, so a machine without it took the weak arm silently on every mint. The same script's session secret had a matching pair — 'openssl rand -hex 32' with a '/dev/urandom | od' fallback — but that one degraded to another CSPRNG rather than to a guessable value, which is why only the id is this entry.
bugs.fix: new_session_id calls plan_random_hex 8, which is the shipped plan-crypt binary (/dev/urandom on unix, BCryptGenRandom on Windows) or, without it, /dev/urandom read directly and length-checked. There is no third arm: without a CSPRNG the helper exits 69 and mints nothing. The session secret moved to plan_random_hex 32 in the same change, which also fixed a width inconsistency — 'openssl rand -hex 32' produced 64 hex chars but its 'head -c 64 /dev/urandom' fallback produced 128, against a comment in both scripts asserting the secret is always 64.
bugs.verification: planning/tests/test-plan-crypt.sh section 6: two draws must differ, 64 consecutive draws must all be distinct, the width must be exactly 2 chars per byte, every character must be hex, and mint-fix-keys.sh must contain no $RANDOM expansion outside a comment. Mutation: replacing plan_random_hex's body with a constant ('printf ab' repeated) makes it report 'two session ids came out identical: abababababababab' and '64 draws are all distinct: expected 64, got 1'. A second mutation in the Rust source — random::fill returning a zeroed buffer instead of reading the OS — fails two cargo tests, draws_differ_and_are_not_zero and odd_lengths_are_filled. Starved-PATH run with no plan-crypt and no digest tool exits 69 rather than improvising.

bugs.title: Nothing requires the coordinator to sanity-check its own plan before dispatching a reviewer, so reviewer cycles are spent on mechanical surface inconsistencies
bugs.reproduce: Draft a plan, get an adversarial review, resolve the findings with update-work-unit.sh and update-plan-content.sh, then dispatch a fresh reviewer. Repeat. Observed over six cycles on .plans/loki-shippinglogic-rewrite (67 work units, 10 goals).
bugs.observed: Every cycle from 2 to 6 was gated by at least one BLOCKING finding that was purely an intra-document inconsistency, each in a surface the previous fix had not touched. Cycle 2: unit Objectives corrected, Instructions and Acceptance criteria left stale - 12 of 20 findings unresolved for that reason alone. Cycle 3: the inverse - Instructions and criteria corrected, inventory row and Objective left stale, so W20 read 'leave dropship buckets unchanged' in its Objective while its own Instructions called that wording 'an earlier version'. Cycle 5: a testing companion whose backend-verification section demanded a rule count its own automated-tests section explained was impossible. Cycle 6: a companion whose browser-verification section told the worker to run and record three user stories the same step's criterion forbids it from recording. Findings ran 20, 12, 5, 8, 3 with blocking 14, 6, 1, 1, 1 - converging, but roughly 800k reviewer tokens across six cycles. A mechanical self-sweep over all 133 step and companion documents, run afterwards, then found two further defects no reviewer had named: a handoff claiming 'the following four steps each add one public method' after a fifth moved in, and a handoff routing per-customer filtering to a goal that no longer performed it.
bugs.expected: The coordinator performs its own coherence pass and resolves what it finds BEFORE spending a reviewer cycle, so the reviewer is spent on judgement - whether a criterion can be satisfied by construction, whether a premise holds against the repository - rather than on consistency sweeps a script can do exhaustively.
bugs.mechanism: SKILL.md section 3 documents the seven surfaces a fix must reach and says to search the plan for the OLD wording, but that discipline is advisory prose inside the finding-resolution guidance. The mandated execution order is write the draft, invoke the fresh reviewer, resolve every finding, invoke a fresh reviewer again - with no self-check gate between resolving and re-dispatching. validate-plan.sh checks structure, ownership, dependency edges and rosters, but nothing intra-document: it cannot see a paragraph that contradicts another paragraph of the same file. The --stale gate is the closest existing mechanism and does not close the loop - it only matches a phrase list the agent supplies from memory, and every hit is a WARN that never changes exit status.
bugs.found_by: Tschallacka, during the Loki checkout migration plan on Sanitairkamer; he stopped the loop and told the agent to check every file itself before dispatching another reviewer.
bugs.notes: Proposed fix has two halves that belong together. First, SKILL.md: make a coordinator self-coherence pass a required step in the execution order, between resolving findings and re-invoking a reviewer. Second, validate-plan.sh: add a mechanical intra-document coherence check, which is the half that makes the requirement enforceable rather than aspirational. Three checks caught every instance seen here and are cheap - flag a document where one paragraph declares wording stale (an earlier version ... said X) while another paragraph of the SAME document still carries X; flag a spelled-out count adjacent to method, limitation, rule, item, type, cart or story, since those drift whenever a unit moves between goals; and flag a testing companion whose sections disagree, which is where cycles 5 and 6 both failed. Why it went unnoticed: each cycle the reviewer correctly reported the inconsistency it found, so the loop looked like it was working. Nobody measured that the SAME defect class was recurring in a new surface each time, which is the signal that the process rather than the plan was at fault. The skill already warns about this in the abstract - it notes a comparable run reaching seventeen cycles and 41.7 million tokens before anyone asked whether the plan was the thing at fault - so the gap is enforcement, not awareness. Coordinator's own retrospective, recorded at Tschallacka's instruction after the reviewer round that followed: (1) I focused my first audits on validator-detectable structure - stale state, propagation, dependencies, rosters and helper consistency. (2) I did not initially perform a complete semantic ownership sweep asking, for every acceptance criterion, which exact executable test proves this and whether that test is owned by exactly one unit. (3) That omission allowed the reviewer to find gaps that were visible from the plan itself; Tschallacka was right to call it out. (4) Process change: before every reviewer dispatch, audit every affected unit's objective, instructions, acceptance, inventory row, companion, dependency, coverage and concrete executable owner - not just run validators. Note that this names a defect class distinct from the intra-document one above: the checks described earlier compare a document against itself, whereas this one asks whether each criterion maps to a single named executable test. validate-plan.sh already checks ownership structurally, so the missing half is semantic - criterion to concrete test, exactly one owner.

bugs.title: A fix-key secret evicted from the temp dir makes every minted key and recorded claim permanently unverifiable, so the plan can never be approved
bugs.reproduce: p=.plans/<plan-with-gated-findings>; planning/scripts/mint-fix-keys.sh "$p"; s=$(sed -n 's/.*"session_id"[[:space:]]*:[[:space:]]*"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$p/fix-keys.json" | head -1); rm -rf "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/planning-agent/review-fix-keys/$s"; planning/scripts/verify-fix-keys.sh "$p" --claimed-by fixer; echo "exit=$?"
bugs.observed: verify-fix-keys.sh: session secret missing: /tmp/planning-agent/review-fix-keys/<session>/secret (was the session invalidated at approval?) and exit=64. The keys still in fix-keys.json and the claims still in fixes.md can never be verified again, so --review-status approved refuses for the rest of the plan's life.
bugs.expected: A mint that survives an ordinary temp-dir eviction, or a documented recovery that restores verifiability without discarding the review. At minimum the refusal should distinguish an evicted secret from a forged key and name the recovery command, rather than asking whether the session was invalidated at approval.
bugs.mechanism: A key is SHA-256(secret || "<session_id>|<finding>|<work unit>") and the 64-hex secret exists only at $(planning_tmpdir)/review-fix-keys/<session>/secret. planning_tmpdir.sh puts that under ${TMPDIR:-/tmp} and its own comment states the intent: it lives there 'so it is fresh per boot'. So the store is designed to be evicted while the protocol it holds spans sessions: minting is the reviewer's step and claiming must be a different session. Once the dir is gone the secret is unrecoverable, verify_fix_keys dies at its secret-file check before the claim loop, and ensure_session_secret silently mints a NEW session on the next call, rewriting fix-keys.json wholesale so prior claims read as stale-key mismatches.
bugs.found_by: coordinator session resuming the plan-overview-rebuild plan; hit twice, first on the 63 keys of cycles 1 to 7 and again on cycle 8's fresh mint across a pause of a few hours
bugs.notes: Unnoticed because every test mints and verifies inside one run, so the secret always exists; nothing exercises a verify whose secret is gone. The error text makes it worse by naming approval-time invalidation as the cause, which is the one documented way the dir disappears, so an ordinary temp eviction reads as a protocol event. The practical consequence for anyone using the gate today is that mint, claim and approve must all complete in one sitting. Recovery is mint-fix-keys.sh, which mints a new session and rewrites the keys, at the cost of every recorded claim and the audit trail of which session claimed which key. The reproduction above is the deliberate form of an eviction that was twice observed accidentally; the observed text and exit code are quoted from those two runs, not from running that command, because deleting a live session secret would break whatever fixer is mid-claim.

So W81's freshness check is free to execute before W78 removes the file, which is the exact case its own handoff says must not happen, and nothing in the suite objects.

It cannot tell a consumption claim from a bare cross-reference by reading prose, so WARN is the right strength -- the same judgement already made for the rule that flags a unit's instructions naming a project symbol no inventory row owns.
bugs.mechanism: validate-plan-propagation-lib.sh carries six checks -- completion, symbols, reach, companion, leaves, freshness, roster -- and not one of them reads a step's `## Handoff` prose. The primitive the check needs is already there and already used: dep_reaches() at validate-plan-propagation-lib.sh:184 computes memoised transitive reachability over the inventory's Depends-on column for the verification-grades-sibling check. So the gap is not missing machinery but a missing application of it: extract the WNN references from each handoff paragraph and run each through dep_reaches in both directions, warning when neither direction reaches. SKILL.md's seven-surface rule names dependency edges (surface 6) and the handoff as separate surfaces to sweep, and nothing cross-checks either against the other.
bugs.found_by: coordinator self-sweep while re-baselining plan-overview-rebuild, run after the cycle-8 reviewer called one instance the fifth recurrence of the class
bugs.notes: Measured, not estimated: 58 of the plan's 118 units carry at least one such handoff claim, spread across 14 of its 17 goals (01-engine-core 11, 02-page-shell 9, 12-adaptive-cinematics 7, 17-build-toolchain 5, 11-visual-language 5, and the rest in ones to fours). Five were read in full to judge precision and all five were genuine consumption claims, not bare references: W02 'W03 and W50 derive from these values'; W101 'W83 and W84 have a flag contract to quote, W14 has the serve and port flags it is invoked through'; W109 'W64, W65 and W66 can carry the marker their audience requires', which is only true after W109 teaches the marker reader the CSS comment form; W78 as quoted above; and W69 'These numbers justify the tier thresholds W71 declares', the one arguable case. Why it went unnoticed: successive reviewers found instances one at a time -- AR-07, AR-21, AR-25, AR-32, AR-53 and AR-67 across six cycles -- and each was correctly reported and closed, so the loop looked healthy while the class was never measured. This is the same failure shape B110 records, and the two are peers rather than parent and child: B110 is about a document contradicting itself and about there being no required coordinator self-check before a reviewer is dispatched, and its proposed checks (stale wording, spelled-out counts, companion sections disagreeing) do not include this one, which compares a document against the dependency graph rather than against itself. A caution for whoever implements it, because two obvious spellings are both wrong and were both tried: comparing against direct Depends-on edges only reports 126 hits on this plan, because ordering is frequently transitive; and a single-pass Floyd-Warshall style relaxation over an awk associative array returned a complete graph (118 squared pairs) whose zero findings looked like a pass. Use real reachability, memoised as dep_reaches already is, and exclude pairs ordered in EITHER direction -- a handoff legitimately names its own upstream, and not excluding upstream adds about thirty false positives. The reproduction above was run as written and produced the quoted observed output verbatim, including validator exit 0. One more exclusion the check needs, measured after the class was swept: it must ignore a unit mentioned inside a paragraph that carries a history marker. SKILL.md requires a corrected paragraph to state what the earlier version said and why it was wrong, so a resolution of this very defect produces sentences like "an earlier version of this paragraph said W82 style rules key off this attribute; W82 rewrites planning/PACKAGE-MAP.tsv and holds no style rules at all". That names W82 while explicitly denying any ordering, and a check that reads unit references without regard to the surrounding retraction will flag it for the life of the plan. The two rules are in direct tension unless the check excludes history-marked paragraphs. Measured on plan-overview-rebuild after the sweep: 58 claims went to 0 genuine, but 14 mentions still flagged -- 11 of them the paragraphs deliberately reworded rather than ordered, and 3 newly created by the rewording itself, one of which reads "that is a scoping note rather than an ordering promise ... so no edge runs between the two in either direction". Every one of the 14 was a reference inside a corrective explanation and none was a defect, so without this exclusion the check reports a permanent floor of false positives proportional to how conscientiously the plan documents its own corrections, which is exactly backwards.

bugs.title: The announce beacon advertises the primary interface address while the server listens only on loopback, so same-machine agents cannot discover it
bugs.reproduce:
AI_CHAT_HOME=$(mktemp -d) CHAT_ANNOUNCE=1 chat-server-rs &  # AI_CHAT_BIND unset -> 127.0.0.1 default
ss -ltn | grep "$(cat $AI_CHAT_HOME/server.port)"
chat-client-rs discover --wait 3 --json

bugs.observed: ss reports LISTEN 127.0.0.1:36819, the beacon reports {"host":"192.168.1.106","port":36819}, and the sibling exits 64 with "no chat server found ... no beacon". A sibling sharing the same AI_CHAT_HOME fails identically.
bugs.expected: A server on the loopback default announces an address a same-machine peer can reach, so a sibling agent with --server omitted connects.
bugs.mechanism: announce_host() (src/chat-server-rs/src/main.rs:965) resolves the advertised host by connecting a UDP socket to 8.8.8.8:80 and reading local_addr, explicitly rejecting a loopback result. It never consults AI_CHAT_BIND, so a loopback-bound server publishes the LAN address it is not listening on. The client then probes that address with tcp_alive (400ms), fails, and the ladder ends. server.port -- written by the server and holding the right port -- is not on the resolution ladder in resolve_server (src/chat-client-rs/src/main.rs:313), so the one authoritative local record is never read.

bugs.title: chat-server-rs stops servicing accepted connections: the broadcast path blocks in write_line while holding hub.writers
bugs.reproduce: start chat-server-rs, attach one live 'chat-client-rs tail --chan #c', then send a dozen messages; watch 'ss -ltn' backlog on the server port
bugs.observed: clients report 'send: Resource temporarily unavailable (os error 11)', sends stop landing in the channel log, and the listener's accept backlog climbs without bound (observed 5 -> 9 -> 11 pending on 127.0.0.1:37251 on 2026-09-04 with two agents in #ai-skills). A message already in flight can land while every later one is lost.
bugs.expected: a slow or dead subscriber never blocks the server: broadcast writes have a write timeout, and accepted connections keep being serviced
bugs.mechanism: Re-measured against a server built from master (06eb743) on 2026-09-04, and the accurate shape is worse than 'the backlog climbs': ONE attached subscriber wedges the server for everyone. src/chat-server-rs/src/main.rs takes hub.writers.lock(), then a second connection's slot, then calls write_line on that connection's socket, and hub.writers is the lock the accept loop needs to register a new connection. But the dominant mechanism is not the blocking write -- it is lock starvation: a subscriber's own thread holds its slot across a 200ms read_tls and re-acquires it immediately, so a broadcaster contending for that slot loses almost every cycle, while holding hub.writers. Measured with one 'chat-client-rs tail' attached: first send 5.7s, next two failed with 'os error 11' after 10.2s each (including a fresh client sending to a DIFFERENT channel), neither appended to any log, main thread in futex_do_wait, server sockets left in CLOSE-WAIT with the unread NICK/USER/PRIVMSG in Recv-Q. A write timeout alone would therefore not have fixed it. The comment claiming 'their slots are different mutexes, so locking them here is safe' is false: safety needs a lock order, not distinct mutexes.
bugs.fix: 991c4bf (branch bug/b122-hub-writers-lock) — each connection gets an outbox: a leaf mutex holding pending lines plus the channel membership a broadcaster needs. A broadcaster copies the peer list under hub.writers, releases it, and appends to each outbox; the connection's own thread drains it and does the socket write. No socket I/O under a shared lock, and no two connection slots locked at once. Plus SO_SNDTIMEO on every accepted socket, write_line returning its error instead of swallowing it (a failed write closes the connection so the existing teardown runs), a byte cap on the outbox that marks an unresponsive peer dead, and PART now updating the broadcast membership (it lived on the connection state, which only JOIN maintained).
bugs.verification: chat/tests/test-chat-broadcast-stall.sh attaches one 'chat-client-rs tail' subscriber and asserts the server keeps serving. All six assertions fail against a server built from master (CHAT_SERVER_BIN points the test at one) with 'os error 11' after ten seconds each, and all six pass with the fix; the run drops from 1m17s of timeouts to 22s. Its precondition -- that the subscriber really is an attached channel member -- is asserted (the subscriber must print a message another client sent) rather than slept for, so it cannot pass vacuously. The outbox policy has four unit tests (membership filter, order and drain-once, the cap marking a peer dead and releasing its backlog, a dead peer never queued for again), each shown to fail under a mutation of the branch it guards. NOT verified end to end: SO_SNDTIMEO actually firing. Forcing a blocked socket write needs more traffic than a test should push -- 3.6MB queued to a SIGSTOP'd peer was absorbed by the kernel with no block, and this host's tcp_rmem max is 32MB -- so the write timeout and the cap are bounds on damage rather than paths the integration test exercises.
bugs.found_by: pr-master (reproduced live in #ai-skills 2026-09-04; originally finding F1 of the PR #18 adversarial review)
bugs.notes: On whether killing the subscriber recovers: pr-master measured that it did not, and only a server restart cleared it. In my reproduction (one tail, master's binary) killing the subscriber DID recover immediately -- the peer's close makes read_tls return Ok(0), so its thread tears the slot down and releases the broadcaster. The variant with no self-recovery is a subscriber that stays alive and stops reading (SIGSTOP), because then nothing tells the server anything is wrong. Both variants are asserted in chat/tests/test-chat-broadcast-stall.sh. Correction to the verification above, found by running the mutation rather than assuming it: making the outbox flush a no-op does NOT fail the integration test, so that test does not cover broadcast delivery. chat-client-rs tail reads new messages with FETCH and ignores PRIVMSG lines outright, so the shipped client never consumes a broadcast; nothing it can do asserts that path end to end. The queueing itself is covered by the four outbox unit tests. Worth knowing separately: the broadcast path that wedged the server is used only by stock IRC clients, not by the agents' own client.

bugs.title: a broadcast PRIVMSG carries no message id, so a push-consuming client cannot maintain an accurate cursor
bugs.reproduce: attach a client that consumes pushed PRIVMSG rather than polling FETCH, then try to record which id it has seen
bugs.observed: the pushed line is ':<nick>!<user>@<host> PRIVMSG #chan :<text>' with no id anywhere, while the FETCH reply carries 'MSG #chan <id> <ts> <nick> :<text>'. So a client that follows the push stream -- which is what T91/T91a require -- has no way to know which id it has consumed, and the only local option is to infer one by counting pushes from the JOIN LASTID. That inference is correct only while nothing is ever lost, reordered or interleaved, and it fails silently otherwise: the cursor drifts and the next reconnect replays or SKIPS messages while appearing to work.
bugs.expected: the pushed line names the id it is delivering, so a push-consuming client can record exactly what it has seen and backfill from that cursor on reconnect without guessing
bugs.mechanism: the broadcaster serialises a chat-proto Message with command PRIVMSG, params [chan] and the text as trailing, which is deliberately the RFC-shaped line a stock IRC client expects; the id lives only in the log record and in the additive FETCH extension's MSG reply. The two paths therefore disagree about what a delivered message is, and only the polling path can drive a cursor. Any fix has to stay wire-compatible with a stock client -- an IRCv3 message tag or a private numeric alongside the PRIVMSG rather than a changed PRIVMSG shape.
bugs.found_by: bug-fixer, while implementing T91a; it asked rather than shipping the counting inference, which is how this surfaced

bugs.title: the perl chat rung collapses all whitespace where the other three map newline to one space
bugs.reproduce: Send a body containing a tab or a run of spaces through each rung in turn and compare the stored log line
bugs.observed: Not measured here; reported by the chatfix subagent from reading the four runtimes. perl does s/\s+/ /g, collapsing every whitespace run to a single space; python3, node and the bash handler map each newline and CR to one space and leave other whitespace alone. The same message body therefore stores differently depending on which rung the host happened to pick.
bugs.expected: A message body stores identically whichever rung is serving, since the rungs are meant to be interchangeable implementations of one protocol.

bugs.found_by: the chatfix subagent
bugs.notes: This was the clearest case of the class: a bug whose entire content is a discrepancy between two implementations stops being a defect the moment one of them is the only one. The four-rung design is what made it possible, and dropping it is what closed it.

bugs.title: chat-client-rs cannot dial a bare IPv6 server address, so an IPv6 bus is unreachable even when discovered
bugs.observed: With the beacon carrying host ::1 the ladder returns ::1:<port> -- tcp_alive accepts it, because Rust's to_socket_addrs splits on the last colon -- and the connect then fails with "chat-client-rs: server name: invalid dns name", exit 70. A bracketed --server [::1]:<port> fails the same way.
bugs.expected: Either an IPv6 address is dialable end to end, or the client refuses it with a message naming IPv6 as the reason rather than reporting an invalid DNS name.
bugs.mechanism: server_host() (src/chat-client-rs/src/main.rs:584-586) takes the host by `server.split(:).next()`, which on an IPv6 literal yields the empty string (or "[" when bracketed). That is handed to ServerName::try_from for TLS SNI, which rejects it. The address never reaches a socket. Splitting on the LAST colon and stripping brackets, or parsing with SocketAddr, is what a v6-aware host extraction needs -- and an IP literal should use ServerName::IpAddress rather than a DNS name at all.
bugs.found_by: an adversarial review of the chat-server-rs announce change (PR #20)
bugs.notes: Not a regression: before the announce change an IPv6 bind advertised an IPv4 address it was not listening on, so an IPv6 bus was unreachable then too. The failure merely moved from "never found" to "found, then rejected at TLS". The server side now refuses to announce a bare IPv6 host and says why, naming this entry, so nothing advertises an address that cannot be used -- that is containment, not a fix. Filed against the client because that is where the extraction lives; src/chat-client-rs/ is being worked on separately for B116, so this is recorded rather than fixed here to avoid two workers in one file. Low priority: no known caller binds IPv6, and the workaround is to bind IPv4 or set CHAT_ANNOUNCE_HOST.
